newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea c/a deficit rises, but positive signs seen.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea c/a deficit rises, but positive signs seen.

text.p: South Korea on Tuesday posted a record current account deficit for the first quarter, but the central bank and economists were optimistic that a recovery in exports would speed up in the months ahead.
"It's better than our expectations and signals the bottom of the economy may be reached earlier than predicted," said Lee Youn-ho, president of the LG Economic Research Institute.
The Bank of Korea announced a $7.94 billion current account deficit for the first three months of this year, sharply up from a $4.64 billion shortfall in the same 1996 period.

In March, the deficit rose 142 percent year-on-year to $2.27 billion, but it was off from February's $2.5 billion deficit. The trade deficit in March also fell month-on-month to $1.4 billion from February's shortfall of $1.83 billion.

Ohn Ki-un, senior fellow at the state-backed Korea Institute for International Economics and Trade, said the figures support the view that the economy would bottom out in the early part of the second half of 1997.
"There will not be any surprise pick-up in the economy, but it will continue to recover," said Ohn.
LG's Lee said he had earlier predicted the economy would hit bottom towards the end of this year.
A senior official at the central bank said March figures supported his optimism that exports, which drive the nation's economy, have been and would continue gaining momentum.
"Exports are recovering steadily while import growth is slowing," Paeng Dong-jun, director of the bank's statistics department, said by telephone.
"Prices for our major export items have rebounded this year and I expect the fruits to materialise later," he said.

Last year, sharp drops in prices for the nation's key export items, especially dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips, pushed the annual current account deficit up to a record $23.72 billion against the $8.95 billion shortfall in 1995.
In March this year, customs-cleared exports fell 2.8 percent to $11.36 billion from a year earlier. The year-on-year drop was a significant slowdown from the 5.3 percent fall in February.
Exports of automobiles, machinery and metallic products rose sharply while the slump in exports of electronic goods persisted, the central bank said.
Economists said exports of petrochemicals, steel products and computer chips would grow steadily for the rest of this year, based on rising global demand.

The government has forecast this year's economic growth, measured by gross domestic product (GDP), would slow to about 5.5 percent from a 7.1 percent gain in 1996. South Korea's GDP rose by 8.9 percent in 1995 and by 8.6 percent in 1994.
Paeng said the central bank was sticking to its forecast for this year's current account deficit to just exceed $18 billion.

On Tuesday, South Korea also recorded 9.1 percent growth year-on-year in its industrial output for March, compared with a 5.8 percent rise a year earlier, while inventories increased 13.8 percent in March versus a 19.1 percent rise a year ago.
The National Statistical Office said the consumer price index (CPI), South Korea's main indicator of inflation, rose 4.3 percent year-on-year in March, down from a 4.6 percent rise in March 1996.
South Korea said it would cap this year's annual CPI growth at about last year's level of 4.5 percent.
The producer price index, which shows future price trends, rose 3.8 percent on the year in March versus growth of 2.0 percent a year earlier.
